claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a therapeutic study in rat models.

claims.claim: Chronic ER stress and autophagy alterations caused by Wfs1 loss results in the acceleration of Tau protein aggregation and relative pathology in mouse hippocampus.
claims.source: Interestingly, chronic ER stress and autophagy alterations caused by Wfs1 loss results in the acceleration of Tau protein aggregation and relative pathology in mouse hippocampus suggesting a novel mechanism by which wolframin deficiency can lead to neurodegeneration (Delpech et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claims.claim: pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age.
claims.source: Whilst pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age (WT: 68±5; Wfs1-KO: 72±6; p<0.05), a prolonged implicit time, which refers to the interval between the stimulation and the peak of the negative response, was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals (WT: 76±5; Wfs1-KO: 82±6; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: A prolonged implicit time was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals.
claims.source: Whilst pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age (WT: 68±5; Wfs1-KO: 72±6; p<0.05), a prolonged implicit time, which refers to the interval between the stimulation and the peak of the negative response, was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals (WT: 76±5; Wfs1-KO: 82±6; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 and 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: This early indication of RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 (WT: 73 ± 6; Wfs1-KO: 83 ± 9; p < 0.05) and 12 (WT: 76 ± 5; Wfs1-KO: 85 ± 5; p < 0.0001) months old mutant mice, with the latter group that showed, beside a delayed response , also a significant PhNR amplitude decrease (WT: 11±2; Wfs1-KO: 8±2, p<0.0001) at the latest time period (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice showed a significant PhNR amplitude decrease.
claims.source: This early indication of RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 (WT: 73 ± 6; Wfs1-KO: 83 ± 9; p < 0.05) and 12 (WT: 76 ± 5; Wfs1-KO: 85 ± 5; p < 0.0001) months old mutant mice, with the latter group that showed, beside a delayed response , also a significant PhNR amplitude decrease (WT: 11±2; Wfs1-KO: 8±2, p<0.0001) at the latest time period (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 2 and 4 months old Wfs1 mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations.
claims.source: While 2 and 4 months old mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations, 8-month-old mutant mice displayed increased latencies (WT: 46±4; Wfs1-KO: 51±2, p<0.001), indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 8-month-old Wfs1 mutant mice displayed increased VEP latencies, indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway.
claims.source: While 2 and 4 months old mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations, 8-month-old mutant mice displayed increased latencies (WT: 46±4; Wfs1-KO: 51±2, p<0.001), indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Both VEP amplitude and latency parameters were significantly affected in 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: However, both VEP parameters were significantly affected as mouse age progressed to 12 months (VEP amplitude WT: 40±14; Wfs1-KO: 28±2; p<0.001; VEP latencies WT: 47±2; Wfs1-KO: 52±3, p<0.001) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age.
claims.source: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age while a significant loss was recorded at 8 months which markedly worsened 4 months later (4 months - WT: 0.40±0.5; Wfs1-KO 0.36±0.8 c/deg, 8 months - WT: 0.39±0.4; Wfs1-KO: 0.30±0.3 c/deg, p<0.05, 12 months - WT: 0.38±0.6; Wfs1-KO: 0.19±0.5 c/deg, p<0.01; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optomotor reflex measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A significant loss of visual acuity was recorded at 8 months in Wfs1 mutant mice which markedly worsened 4 months later.
claims.source: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age while a significant loss was recorded at 8 months which markedly worsened 4 months later (4 months - WT: 0.40±0.5; Wfs1-KO 0.36±0.8 c/deg, 8 months - WT: 0.39±0.4; Wfs1-KO: 0.30±0.3 c/deg, p<0.05, 12 months - WT: 0.38±0.6; Wfs1-KO: 0.19±0.5 c/deg, p<0.01; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optomotor reflex measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The initial visual impairment in Wfs1 mutant mice is represented by RGC alterations in the retinal tissue followed by a delay of the visual stimulus along the nerve fibers.
claims.source: These results imply that the initial visual impairment in Wfs1 mutant mice is represented by RCG alterations in the retinal tissue followed by a delay of the visual stimulus along the nerve fibers suggesting a progressive optic nerve damage.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of pERG and VEP alterations.

claims.claim: RGC functions are extensively altered causing a drastic loss of visual acuity at 12 months of age in Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: Subsequently, RGC functions are extensively altered causing a drastic loss of visual acuity at 12 months of age.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined pERG, VEP, and optomotor reflex data at 12 months.

claims.claim: OCT and fluorescein angiography did not reveal any signs of retinal vasculature dysfunction in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: FA assessment was necessary to exclude confounding effects due to diabetic retinopathy (DM), which represents one of the major eye complications of DM but whose causative mechanisms are highly different from those in WS1 (Hilson et al., 2009). The collected images did not reveal any signs of retinal vasculature dysfunction in either group of animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCT and FA imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: OCT-angiography did not highlight any significant difference in the eye fundi or perfusion and vessel length density and tortuosity in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: Indeed, OCT-angiography did not highlight any significant difference in the eye fundi or perfusion and vessel length density and tortuosity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCT-angiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: No significant differences in RNFL thickness were disclosed by structural OCT in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: Moreover, we also assessed the thickness of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and no significant differences were disclosed by structural OCT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCT measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Three 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice did not show big abnormalities in RNFL thickness at OCT segmentation.
claims.source: Since mutant elderly mice often displayed corneal haze, with consequent poor quality images, we managed to sample only three 12 months old clear-lensed eyes that still did not show big abnormalities in RNFL thickness at OCT segmentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCT measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 8 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves presented incipient myelin thinning with reduced myelin area and a higher proportion of empty space, but without axonal count discrepancies.
claims.source: These elaborations revealed that 8 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves presented incipient myelin thinning (g-ratio - WT: 0.52±0.18; Wfs1-KO: 0.54±0.14, p<0.05) with reduced myelin area and a higher proportion of empty space, but without axonal count discrepancies (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: TEM imaging in 12 months old Wfs1 mutant animals unveiled signs of more severe myelin degeneration with pathological features and degenerating fibers.
claims.source: TEM imaging in elderly mutant animals (12 months of age) unveiled signs of more severe myelin degeneration (g-ratio - WT: 0.42±0.18; Wfs1-KO: 0.50±0,18, p<0.05) with pathological features and degenerating fibers (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 12 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves showed a significant reduction of axonal density and area occupied by myelin together with evident signs of axonal damage with increased g-ratio.
claims.source: In particular, we observed a significant reduction of axonal density and area occupied by myelin together with evident signs of axonal damage with increased g-ratio (WT: 0.41±0.04; Wfs1-KO: 0.51±0.003, p<0.05; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Myelin alterations and axonal thinning are the first pathological signs followed by manifested myelin degeneration and axonal loss in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that myelin alterations and axonal thinning are the first pathological signs followed by manifested myelin degeneration and axonal loss in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of TEM findings at 8 and 12 months.

claims.claim: The pathological progression in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves is perfectly matching the timeline of the visual functional deficits previously uncovered by electrophysiological recordings and the optomotor analysis.
claims.source: This pathological progression is perfectly matching the timeline of the visual functional deficits previously uncovered by electrophysiological recordings and the optomotor analysis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred by comparing the temporal progression of structural and functional deficits.

claims.claim: Unbiased stereology counting did not reveal significant RGC number changes in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
claims.source: Unbiased stereology counting did not reveal significant RGC number changes in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RBPMS immunostaining and cell counting shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The loss of the RGC population became evident and statistically relevant at 12 months in Wfs1 mutant mice (28% ± 6% loss in Wfs1-KO vs WT retinas).
claims.source: However, 4 months later the loss of the RGC population became evident and statistically relevant (28% ± 6% loss in Wfs1-KO vs WT retinas) indicating a progressive loss of RGC somata over time (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RBPMS immunostaining and cell counting shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Axonal damage and myelin degeneration anticipate the frank loss of RGC cell bodies in the retinas.
claims.source: These results illustrate that axonal damage and myelin degeneration anticipate the frank loss of RGC cell bodies in the retinas, even if within a relative delayed time frame a severe loss of RGCs can be also detectable in the Wfs1-deficient retinas.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression showing optic nerve damage at 8 months and RGC loss at 12 months.

claims.claim: t-SNE analysis of the RNA-seq datasets confirmed the expected closer similarity and correlation between all mutant retinas in comparison to the analogous wild-type samples.
claims.source: t-SNE analysis of the RNA-seq datasets confirmed the expected closer similarity and correlation between all mutant retinas in comparison to the analogous wild-type samples (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Computational analysis identified 396 genes differentially expressed (DEGs) in mutant retinas compared to the control counterparts, with a similar proportion of either up- or downregulated genes.
claims.source: Computational analysis identified 396 genes differentially expressed (DEGs) in mutant retinas compared to the control counterparts, with a similar proportion of either up- or downregulated genes (Figure 3B), suggesting not profound transcriptome alterations but rather selective changes in mutant samples at this stage.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Gene enrichment analysis revealed many deregulated genes related to pathways like cell death, UPR response and protein folding.
claims.source: Interestingly, gene enrichment analysis (Gene Ontology, GO) revealed many deregulated genes related to pathways like cell death, UPR response and protein folding (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: All pathways related to cell death, UPR response and protein folding were down-regulated in the mutant retinas.
claims.source: Intriguingly, all these pathways were down-regulated in the mutant retinas, in line with the general assumption from literature that wolframin loss impairs the cellular stress-coping capacities.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis and is consistent with literature on wolframin function.

claims.claim: Mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways.
claims.source: On the contrary, mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways (Figure 3C) as those associated with reactive glial cells like, Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 (Figure 3D; Liu et al., 2022; Linnerbauer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: Genes associated with reactive glial cells like Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 were upregulated in mutant retinas.
claims.source: On the contrary, mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways (Figure 3C) as those associated with reactive glial cells like, Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 (Figure 3D; Liu et al., 2022; Linnerbauer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and citations to literature.

claims.claim: Immunocytochemical analysis confirmed the aberrant activation of the ER stress effectors ATF6 and CHOP in mutant retinal samples.
claims.source: We, next, performed immunocytochemical analysis confirming the aberrant activation of the ER stress effectors ATF6 (WT: 0.5±0.3; Wfs1-KO: 1.5±0.2) and CHOP (WT: 0.2±0.01; Wfs1-KO: 0.4±0.02) in mutant retinal samples (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: GFAP staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age.
claims.source: Moreover, GFAP (8 months WT: 0.5±0.2; Wfs1-KO: 1.4±0.3; 12 months WT: 0.2±0.02; Wfs1-KO: 52±2) and Vimentin (VIM) (8 months WT: 20±2; Wfs1-KO: 38±5; 12 months WT: 2.2±0.5; Wfs1-KO: 4.6±0.8) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Vimentin (VIM) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age.
claims.source: Moreover, GFAP (8 months WT: 0.5±0.2; Wfs1-KO: 1.4±0.3; 12 months WT: 0.2±0.02; Wfs1-KO: 52±2) and Vimentin (VIM) (8 months WT: 20±2; Wfs1-KO: 38±5; 12 months WT: 2.2±0.5; Wfs1-KO: 4.6±0.8) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The glia-specific glutamine synthetase (GS) enzyme was found downregulated both at mRNA and protein levels in Wfs1-deficient retinas.
claims.source: Furthermore, the glia-specific glutamine synthetase (GS) enzyme was found downregulated both at mRNA and protein levels in Wfs1-deficient retinas (Figures 3C and 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 3C and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: GS reduction in Wfs1-deficient retinal glial cells might favor a toxic environment detrimental for neuronal survival.
claims.source: GS generates glutamine by assembling glutamate and ammonia and, therefore, having a critical role in preventing glutamate-dependent excitotoxicity and ammonia toxicity (Rose et al., 2013). Thus, GS reduction in Wfs1-deficient retinal glial cells might favor a toxic environment detrimental for neuronal survival.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of GS and its reduction in mutant retinas.

claims.claim: The genes encoding for the key neurotrophic molecule BDNF, and the survival factors Nr4a1 and Nr4a3 were reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
claims.source: Next, the genes encoding for the key neurotrophic molecule BDNF, and the survival factors Nr4a1 and Nr4a3 were also reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas (Figure 3D), further altering neuronal homeostasis and stress resilience.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: BDNF is expressed by RGCs and Müller glia in adulthood retina, where it exerts its autocrine or paracrine effects.
claims.source: In fact, BDNF is a well-known neurotrophic factor expressed by RGCs and Müller glia in adulthood retina, where it exerts its autocrine or paracrine effects.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about BDNF expression and function in the retina.

claims.claim: BDNF promotes survival of RGCs and can ameliorate RGC death after traumatic optic nerve injury.
claims.source: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that BDNF promotes survival of RGCs and can ameliorates RGC death after traumatic optic nerve injury (Bennett et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claims.claim: Levels of interferon-inducible genes and NF-κB signaling components were unchanged in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
claims.source: However, levels of interferon-inducible genes and NF-κB signaling components were unchanged suggesting the lack of a generalized inflammatory response, but rather a selective activation of specific neuro-inflammatory pathways.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA-seq data showing selective upregulation of inflammatory genes.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR analysis on independent biological samples substantially confirmed the transcriptome data for the key selected genes.
claims.source: To further strengthen our results, RT-qPCR analysis were performed on independent biological samples and substantially confirmed the transcriptome data for the key selected genes (Figure 3E), further highlighting a selective pro-inflammatory profile in Wfs1-deficient retinas.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The dysregulated Lcn2 and Vim genes in Wfs1 mutant samples have been shown to be direct targets of the STAT3 signaling.
claims.source: On this line, we noted that the dysregulated Lcn2 and Vim genes in Wsf1 mutant samples have been shown to be direct targets of the STAT3 signaling (Herrmann et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claims.claim: STAT3 can be stimulated by the ER stress-dependent PERK and IRE1α pathways in glial and cancer cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, previous studies reported that STAT3 can be stimulated by the ER stress-dependent PERK and IRE1α pathways in glial and cancer cells (Meares et al., 2014; Chen and Zhang, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature.

claims.claim: The active STAT3 variant (pY705) was highly enhanced in Wfs1 mutant retinal samples.
claims.source: Interestingly, the active STAT3 variant was highly enhanced in mutant samples although with some variability among the samples (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: STAT3 regulated genes such as Fgf2, Il6, Vegfa, C1s, and C1rl were consistently upregulated in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
claims.source: Thus, we profiled by candidate gene expression other STAT3 regulated genes such as Fgf2, Il6, Vegfa, C1s, and C1rl finding them consistently upregulated in Wfs1 mutant retinas (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: A prominent pro-inflammatory molecular program associated with reduction of survival and homeostatic factors is promoted at least in part by the ER stress-dependent STAT3 activation in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
claims.source: Altogether, these findings uncovered a prominent pro-inflammatory molecular program associated with reduction of survival and homeostatic factors which is promoted at least in part by the ER stress-dependent STAT3 activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing ER stress, STAT3 activation, and inflammatory gene upregulation.

claims.claim: Label-free LC-MS comparative proteomics identified 2046 proteins in retinal samples.
claims.source: Overall, 2046 proteins were identified (Supplementary file 1) and the virtual 2D map showed the ability of the shotgun approach to identify proteins in a wide range of molecular weight and isoelectrical point (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The quantitative analysis led to the identification of 21 differentially expressed proteins between the two genotypes with 9 upregulated and 12 downregulated in the Wfs1-KO compared to the WT condition.
claims.source: The quantitative analysis, combined with statistical evaluation, led to the identification of 21 differentially expressed proteins between the two genotypes with 9 upregulated and 12 downregulated in the Wfs1-KO compared to the WT condition (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The most upregulated protein upon Wfs1 gene loss was GFAP.
claims.source: Notably, the most upregulated protein upon Wfs1 gene loss was GFAP, confirming increased gliosis described earlier in the mutant retinas (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Among the most downregulated molecules in mutant samples, MCT1 (Slc16a1) and basigin were identified.
claims.source: Conversely, among the most downregulated molecules in mutant samples, we identified MCT1 (Slc16a1) and basigin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: MCT1 belongs to the family of monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) that promotes the transport across cell membranes and the shuttling between cells of energy metabolites as lactate, pyruvate or ketone bodies.
claims.source: MCT1 belongs to the family of monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) that promotes the transport across cell membranes and the shuttling between cells of energy metabolites as lactate, pyruvate or ketone bodies (Felmlee et al., 2020; Bosshart et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MCT1 function supported by citations.

claims.claim: Basigin is a glycoprotein which assembles with MCT1 promoting its trafficking from ER and its stabilization on the cell membrane.
claims.source: Basigin (known also as CD147) is a glycoprotein which assembles with MCT1 promoting its trafficking from ER and its stabilization on the cell membrane (Kirk et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about basigin function supported by citation.

claims.claim: In brain, MCTs govern the extracellular release of lactate from glycolytic astrocytes and its transfer into neurons where it is oxidized to generate ATP.
claims.source: In brain, MCTs govern the extracellular release of lactate from glycolytic astrocytes and its transfer into neurons where it is oxidized to generate ATP (Brooks, 2018; Magistretti and Allaman, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle supported by citations.

claims.claim: Western blotting confirmed a strong downregulation of MCT1 in Wfs1 mutant retinas both at 5 and 8 months of age.
claims.source: To confirm the proteomics results, western blotting for MCT1 was performed on independent retinal tissue samples confirming a strong downregulation of this transporter both at 5 and 8 months of age (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: A marked reduction of basigin was detectable in mutant retinas at 5 months of age.
claims.source: Similarly, a marked reduction of basigin was detectable in mutant retinas at 5 months of age (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: MCT2 levels were found upregulated in 8 months old mutant retinas.
claims.source: In contrast, MCT2 levels were found upregulated in 8 months old mutant retinas (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Loss of MCT1 and basigin is detectable months in advance respect to the frank degeneration.
claims.source: Thus, loss of MCT1 and basigin is detectable months in advance respect to the frank degeneration suggesting that the pathological process proceeds with a relatively slow progression before leading to clinically relevant symptoms.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1/basigin loss occurs at 5-8 months while RGC loss occurs at 12 months.

claims.claim: MCT1 loss was detectable also in brain cortical and striatal tissue samples in 8 months old Wfs1-deficient mice.
claims.source: Intriguingly, MCT1 loss was detectable also in brain cortical and striatal tissue samples in 8 months old Wfs1-deficient mice (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: MCT1 protein levels were strongly downregulated in WFS1-deficient HeLa cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, MCT1 protein levels were strongly downregulated in WFS1-deficient HeLa cells, but not in equivalent cells that underwent the same technical procedures but without the successful inactivation of WFS1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in WFS1 knockout HeLa cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The wolframin-dependent regulation of MCT1 protein levels is not restricted only to the retina but is a more general phenomenon.
claims.source: These results suggest that the wolframin-dependent regulation of MCT1 protein levels is not restricted only to the retina but is a more general phenomenon.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1 is reduced in both retina and brain, and in HeLa cells upon WFS1 knockout.

claims.claim: MCT1-V5 was efficiently retrieved from the Wfs1-mCherry immunoprecipitated samples indicating that the two proteins can interact together.
claims.source: Interestingly, MCT1-V5 was efficiently retrieved from the Wfs1-mCherry immunoprecipitated samples indicating that the two proteins can interact together (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Wfs1 and Slc16a1 were found predominantly co-expressed in glial and photoreceptor cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, Wfs1 and Slc16a1 were found predominantly co-expressed in glial and photoreceptor cells (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Expression of Slc16a7, encoding for MCT2, was restricted to the retinal neuronal lineage.
claims.source: Conversely, expression of Slc16a7, encoding for MCT2, was restricted to the retinal neuronal lineage similarly to its selective cell type expression in the brain (Figure 7A; Pierre and Pellerin, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A and citation to literature.

claims.claim: Both wolframin and MCT1 proteins were detectable in lysates of isolated optic nerves.
claims.source: We also confirmed that both wolframin and MCT1 proteins were detectable in lysates of isolated optic nerves (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Wolframin and MCT1 were mainly localized in MBP positive oligodendrocytes wrapping the axonal fibers.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence analysis on optic nerve sections revealed that wolframin and MCT1 were mainly localized in MBP positive oligodendrocytes wrapping the axonal fibers (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Myelin sheaths play a key role in glial-axonal metabolic support by shuttling metabolites like lactate and pyruvate toward axons to fuel the local energy demand.
claims.source: Seminal findings have shown that myelin sheaths play a key role in glial-axonal metabolic support by shuttling metabolites like lactate and pyruvate toward axons to fuel the local energy demand (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to seminal studies.

claims.claim: This trophic support is mediated by both MCT1 and MCT2 localized into oligodendroglia and axons, respectively.
claims.source: This trophic support is mediated by both MCT1 and MCT2 localized into oligodendroglia and axons, respectively (Halestrap and Price, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: MCT1 specific inactivation in oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells leads to late-onset axonal degeneration.
claims.source: This process is crucial for energy homeostasis since MCT1 specific inactivation in oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells leads to late-onset axonal degeneration (Jha et al., 2020; Philips et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing the consequences of MCT1 loss.

claims.claim: Wfs1 gene loss might affect MCT1 protein levels in the optic nerve myelin and the transfer of lactate within the axonal tracts.
claims.source: Thus, it is plausible that Wfs1 gene loss might affect MCT1 protein levels in the optic nerve myelin and the transfer of lactate within the axonal tracts.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed MCT1 reduction and its known function in lactate transfer.

claims.claim: Lactate should accumulate in oligoglial cells that are not able to metabolize themselves the large intracellular quantities if MCT1 is lost.
claims.source: If this is the case, it is expected that lactate should accumulate in oligoglial cells that are not able to metabolize themselves the large intracellular quantities.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of MCT1 in lactate export.

claims.claim: Biochemical quantifications showed a prominent accumulation of lactate in Wfs1 mutant retinas and optic nerves.
claims.source: Biochemical quantifications in both retinas and isolated optic nerves showed a prominent accumulation of lactate in Wfs1 mutant samples (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lactate measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: ATP levels were found significantly downregulated in Wfs1 mutant optic nerve and retinal lysates.
claims.source: In fact, ATP levels were found significantly downregulated in Wfs1 mutant optic nerve and retinal lysates (Figure 7E).

results.result: Wfs1 mutant mice develop progressive visual impairments characterized by early retinal electrophysiological deficits (pERG abnormalities starting at 4 months), followed by optic nerve conduction delays (VEP alterations at 8 months), and culminating in marked visual acuity loss (optomotor reflex deficits at 8-12 months).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C57 provide comprehensive electrophysiological and behavioral data across multiple timepoints (2, 4, 8, and 12 months) with appropriate statistical analyses. The temporal progression from RGC dysfunction to optic nerve impairment to visual loss is well-documented with quantitative measurements and p-values. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=15 for electrophysiology, n=8 for optomotor) and appropriate statistical tests were used.

results.result: Axonal and myelin damage in the optic nerve precedes RGC soma loss in the retina. TEM analysis reveals myelin thinning and increased g-ratio at 8 months without RGC loss, while frank axonal degeneration and 28% RGC loss occur by 12 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C69 are supported by quantitative TEM morphometry showing progressive optic nerve pathology (g-ratio changes, myelin area reduction) at 8 months, while stereological RGC counts (C67-C68) demonstrate preserved cell numbers at 8 months but significant loss (28±6%) at 12 months. The temporal dissociation between axonal and somatic pathology is clearly demonstrated with appropriate quantification and statistics.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis at the pre-degenerative stage (8 months) reveals STAT3-dependent activation of pro-inflammatory glial markers (GFAP, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, C4) with concurrent downregulation of stress-response pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C91 are supported by RNA-seq data (396 DEGs, n=3 per group), GO enrichment analysis, RT-qPCR validation on independent samples, immunofluorescence confirmation of protein changes, and western blot demonstration of increased pSTAT3. The connection to STAT3 is supported by literature citations (C87-C88) and direct measurement of STAT3 activation (C89). The multi-modal validation strengthens the findings.

results.result: Glutamine synthetase (GS) is reduced at both mRNA and protein levels in Wfs1 mutant retinas, potentially creating a toxic environment through impaired glutamate clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 3C) and immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 4D) showing GS reduction at both 8 and 12 months. The mechanistic interpretation (C80) is reasonably inferred from established GS function in glutamate metabolism, though direct measurement of glutamate levels would strengthen the claim.

results.result: BDNF and survival factors Nr4a1 and Nr4a3 are reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas, potentially compromising neuronal homeostasis and RGC survival.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 3D) showing reduced expression of these neurotrophic/survival factors. Claims C82-C83 provide established context for BDNF function in RGC survival. However, the causal link between BDNF reduction and RGC loss is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Label-free proteomics identifies significant reduction of MCT1 and its partner basigin in Wfs1 mutant retinas at 8 months, with MCT1 loss detectable as early as 5 months and confirmed by western blot. MCT2 shows compensatory upregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C102 are supported by comprehensive proteomics analysis (2046 proteins identified, 21 differentially expressed, n=3 per group with technical triplicates) and independent validation by western blot at multiple timepoints (5 and 8 months). The early detection of MCT1/basigin loss (5-8 months) preceding RGC loss (12 months) is well-documented. Statistical significance is reported for key findings.

results.result: MCT1 and wolframin are co-expressed in retinal glia and myelin-forming oligodendrocytes in the optic nerve, as demonstrated by scRNA-seq analysis and immunofluorescence colocalization with MBP.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by analysis of published scRNA-seq data (GSE153673) showing Wfs1 and Slc16a1 co-expression in glial and photoreceptor cells (Figure 7A), western blot detection in optic nerve lysates (Figure 7B), and immunofluorescence colocalization with MBP (Figures 7C and supplement). The cellular localization is well-established through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: Loss of MCT1 causes failure in lactate transfer from glia to neurons/axons, leading to lactate accumulation in glial cells and ATP depletion in both retina and optic nerve, creating a chronic hypometabolic state.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are directly supported by biochemical measurements showing lactate accumulation and ATP reduction in both retinal and optic nerve lysates from Wfs1 mutants (Figures 7D-E with statistical significance). Claims C114-C115, C118-C119 represent reasonable mechanistic inferences based on established MCT1 function in lactate shuttling, though direct measurement of lactate flux would provide stronger evidence.

results.result: The bioenergetic impairment occurs concurrently in both RGC cell bodies and axons months before frank degeneration, selectively endangering RGCs due to their unique high metabolic demands from long myelinated axons.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is well-supported by the temporal data showing MCT1 loss at 5-8 months versus RGC loss at 12 months. Claims C9 and C118 are supported by metabolic measurements in both retina and optic nerve. Claim C120-C121 represents a reasonable inference about RGC selective vulnerability based on their unique anatomy (long myelinated axons) compared to other retinal neurons, though this selectivity is not directly tested experimentally.

results.result: MCT1 loss occurs broadly beyond the retina (brain cortex, striatum, and WFS1-knockout HeLa cells), and wolframin physically interacts with MCT1 as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by western blot data in brain tissues and CRISPR-generated WFS1-KO HeLa cells (Figures 6D and supplement 2). Claim C106 is supported by co-IP experiments showing MCT1-V5 retrieval with Wfs1-mCherry (Figure 6E). However, the co-IP was performed in overexpression conditions in HEK293 cells, which may not fully reflect endogenous interactions. The broader tissue distribution strengthens the generalizability of findings.

results.result: OCT and fluorescein angiography reveal no retinal vasculature dysfunction or significant RNFL thickness changes in Wfs1 mutant mice at 8 months, ruling out diabetic retinopathy as a confounding factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by OCT, OCT-angiography, and FA imaging data (Figure 1 supplement 1) showing no vascular abnormalities or RNFL thinning at 8 months. The limited sample size at 12 months (n=3) due to corneal haze is acknowledged. This negative result is important for excluding diabetic retinopathy as a confounding mechanism.

results.result: Clinical data from WS1 patients shows RNFL thickness decline precedes RGC soma atrophy by approximately a decade, converging with mouse findings to highlight axonal damage as the first disease sign.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by citation to recent clinical study (Barboni et al., 2022). The convergence between mouse and human data strengthens the translational relevance of the findings, though the authors are relying on external clinical data rather than generating it themselves.

results.result: Chronic bioenergetic failure represents an unprecedented new pathological mechanism underlying selective RGC loss and visual impairment in WS1.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is supported by the novel findings of MCT1 loss, lactate accumulation, and ATP depletion in Wfs1 mutant mice. While ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction were previously known in WS1, the specific MCT1-mediated metabolic failure represents a new mechanistic insight. The claim of being 'unprecedented' is reasonable given the novelty of the MCT1 connection.

results.result: Neuroinflammation and MCT1-dependent energy insufficiency may represent independent phenomena that synergistically impair oligodendrocyte metabolic support through inflammation-induced loss of astrocyte-oligodendrocyte gap junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 are largely speculative. While C132-C133 are supported by literature citations about inflammation effects on gap junctions, the proposed synergistic interaction (C135) between inflammation and MCT1 loss is not directly tested. The authors acknowledge this is speculative ('likely two independent phenomena'). Additional experiments would be needed to establish this mechanistic connection.

results.result: Multiple potential mechanisms could explain MCT1/basigin loss upon wolframin deficiency, including impaired vesicle trafficking, reduced membrane stability, ER stress effects, or disrupted oligomeric assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 represent speculative hypotheses about mechanisms linking wolframin to MCT1 regulation. While C139 is supported by citation to prior work on Na+/K+ ATPase, none of these mechanisms are directly tested in the current study. The co-IP data (C106) suggests physical interaction but doesn't distinguish between these mechanistic possibilities. These remain hypotheses for future investigation.

results.result: MCT1 loss likely contributes to broader WS1 symptoms beyond vision, including brain neurodegeneration and sensory peripheral neuropathy, based on MCT1's role in brain and peripheral nerve metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claim C140 is supported by demonstration of MCT1 loss in brain (C103), and claims C141-C145 are supported by literature citations. However, the causal connection between MCT1 loss and these broader symptoms (C142) is speculative and not directly tested. The authors acknowledge this requires 'future studies' to determine. The inference is reasonable but remains unproven.

results.result: Gene therapy strategies should target glial cells rather than RGCs to restore metabolic support, and pharmacological approaches boosting alternative energy substrates represent promising therapeutic directions for WS1.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 represent therapeutic implications and recommendations based on the study findings. While the logic follows from the data showing glial MCT1 loss as a key mechanism, these therapeutic predictions are speculative and not experimentally tested. Claim C146 about RGC-targeted gene therapy being insufficient is a prediction, not a demonstrated result. These represent reasonable future directions but lack experimental validation.

results.result: Background information on WS1 clinical features, WFS1 gene function, known pathogenic mechanisms (ER stress, calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction), and existing animal models establishes the context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C46 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. These provide necessary background context but are not novel findings from the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the background accurately represents current understanding of WS1 pathophysiology and available models.

results.result: Interferon-inducible genes and NF-κB signaling components remain unchanged in Wfs1 mutant retinas, indicating selective rather than generalized inflammatory activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing selective upregulation of specific inflammatory genes without broad inflammatory pathway activation. While not explicitly shown as a figure, this negative result is important for characterizing the inflammatory response as selective. The inference appears reasonable from the presented data.

results.result: Established knowledge about MCT1/basigin function in lactate shuttling and the consequences of MCT1 loss in other models provides mechanistic context for interpreting the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98, C111-C113, C122-C125 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide essential mechanistic context for understanding the significance of MCT1 loss in the Wfs1 model. The citations to prior MCT1 studies in other neurodegenerative contexts (C124) strengthen the translational relevance.
